analysis.one_liner: Requires employers to let workers earn up to a week of paid sick time a year.
analysis.headline: Introduced February 2026 with 156 cosponsors, every one a House Democrat; referred to three committees and never scheduled for a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill requires nearly every employer to let workers earn one hour of paid sick time for every 30 hours worked, capped at 56 hours (about seven workdays) a year. Workers can use the time for their own illness or medical care, to care for a child, parent, spouse, or partner, or to handle domestic violence, sexual assault, or stalking. The Labor Department and private lawsuits would enforce it, and more generous state or employer policies stay in place. Employers that already offer an equivalent policy owe nothing extra.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who do not already have paid sick leave — disproportionately hourly, part-time, and lower-wage employees — plus anyone who needs time to care for a sick family member or to deal with domestic violence or stalking. Under the bill they would earn paid time off for the first time, protected from retaliation.

how_it_helps.text: Workers earn one hour of paid sick time for every 30 hours worked, up to 56 hours a year, starting from their first day on the job and usable after 60 days of employment.

The time can be used for the worker's own physical or mental illness, injury, or medical or preventive care, to care for a child, parent, spouse, domestic partner, or equivalent family member, or to seek medical care, counseling, relocation, or legal help after domestic violence, sexual assault, or stalking.

Employers are barred from firing, demoting, or retaliating against workers who use the time, from counting it against no-fault attendance policies, and from making workers find their own shift replacement as a condition of taking it.

The bill is enforceable through Labor Department investigations and by workers themselves in court, with lost wages, interest, liquidated damages, and attorney's fees available, and employers must keep compliance records and post notice of the rights.

The bill does not preempt state or local laws that provide more generous sick leave, and does not weaken any collective bargaining agreement or employer policy that is more protective than the federal floor.

analysis.who_pays: Employers, who pay wages for hours not worked and bear recordkeeping and compliance costs. The burden falls hardest on businesses that currently offer no paid sick leave — typically smaller operations in low-wage service work — while employers with equivalent existing policies owe nothing extra under the bill.

drawbacks.text: Employers pay wages for hours not worked and must track accrual and use; for small, thin-margin businesses the cost is proportionally largest, since they are the least likely to already offer paid leave.
A doctor's note is only required when the absence covers more than three consecutive workdays, which employers who object to the mandate point to as leaving shorter absences largely unverified.
Accrual is capped at 56 hours a year, and workers who leave a job are not paid out for unused time, so the guarantee is a floor, not a bank account.

Because the bill defers to any more generous state or employer policy and exempts employers whose existing policies already qualify, it raises the standard only where none exists, leaving uneven coverage between states.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers, the benefits are substantial and concrete: paid time to recover from illness or care for a sick child without losing pay or a job, which matters most to the hourly and lower-wage workers least likely to have it. The costs are real but bounded — leave is capped at seven days a year, applies only to hours actually worked, and employers already offering an equivalent policy are exempt. The strongest good-faith objection is the burden on small employers who have never offered paid leave and would absorb wage and compliance costs at once; the bill's three-day certification rule is the other honest sticking point. On balance this is a straightforward labor standard whose costs fall on employers and whose benefits accrue to workers.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in February 2026 and sent to three House committees, and none of them has taken it up, so it is still waiting with no vote scheduled.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the House on February 12, 2026, by Representative Rosa DeLauro of Connecticut with 156 original cosponsors.
All 156 cosponsors are Democrats; no House Republican has signed on.

The House referred the bill to the Education and Workforce Committee, and additionally to the Committees on House Administration and Oversight and Government Reform; the action history shows no hearing, markup, or floor action since.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has had to do anything: employers that do not provide paid sick leave continue under the status quo, and the bill has not advanced far enough to change anyone's situation.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: So far, the status quo holds

for.name: Rosa DeLauro
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Healthy Families Act in the House on February 12, 2026, the latest version of a paid-sick-leave bill she has carried for years.

for.name: 156 House Democratic cosponsors
for.role: Members of the House minority who signed the bill at introduction
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, giving it a large bloc of formal support in one party but none in the other.

against.name: House Education and Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on February 12, 2026; the action history shows no hearing, markup, or vote scheduled since.

sides.party_line_note: Every one of the bill's 156 cosponsors is a House Democrat, and no Republican has signed on, so the bill would need committees and a floor controlled by the opposing party to move.

industries.industry: Restaurants, retail, and other low-wage service employers
industries.note: These businesses are the least likely to already provide paid sick leave, so the bill's requirement to pay wages for leave not worked lands on them first; that cost is precisely the paid time off their employees would gain.

industries.industry: Large employers that already provide comparable paid leave
industries.note: The bill treats any existing policy that meets the floor as fully sufficient, so these employers owe nothing new — it ratifies paid sick leave as an employer-controlled benefit rather than creating a publicly provided alternative.

analysis.trajectory: With no Republican cosponsors and a House majority whose committees set the calendar, the bill is very likely to stay in committee without a hearing or vote and expire at the end of the 119th Congress, as previous versions of the Healthy Families Act have.
